served.stem: Two keto acids are considered for thermal decarboxylation: the gamma-keto acid shown (4-oxopentanoic / levulinic acid) and 3-oxo-3-phenylpropanoic acid (a beta-keto acid). Which statement is correct?
choices: The gamma-keto acid decarboxylates faster, because the extra distance between its carbonyl and its carboxyl relieves strain in the cyclic transition state that delivers the proton
Both decarboxylate equally well because both contain a ketone
Neither decarboxylates; a ketone cannot assist loss of CO2
Only the gamma-keto acid decarboxylates, because only its carbonyl and carboxyl are spaced to close a ring, and the product is a cyclic lactone rather than a simple ketone
Only the beta-keto acid decarboxylates readily on heating; the gamma-keto acid does not, because its carbonyl is too far for a six-membered cyclic transition state
served.bankWhy: Facile thermal decarboxylation requires the second carbonyl to be beta to the carboxyl so a six-membered cyclic transition state can form. The beta-keto acid satisfies this; in the gamma-keto acid the ketone is one carbon too far, so no low-energy cyclic TS exists.

answer.text: Only the beta-keto acid decarboxylates readily on heating; the gamma-keto acid does not, because its carbonyl is too far for a six-membered cyclic transition state
answer.line: Easy loss of CO2 needs a C=O beta to the acid, so the H passes through a six-membered ring. Only the beta-keto acid has that.

steps: Draw the ring the H travels through: the acid H, its O, the carboxyl carbon, the alpha carbon, the ketone carbon and the ketone O. Six atoms.
Count it for each acid. The beta-keto acid closes six; the gamma-keto acid would need seven, and its geometry does not fit.
So only the beta-keto acid loses CO2 on warming, through an enol that becomes acetophenone. Levulinic acid keeps its carboxyl.

choices.text: The gamma-keto acid decarboxylates faster, because the extra distance between its carbonyl and its carboxyl relieves strain in the cyclic transition state that delivers the proton
choices.note: The six-membered ring is already strain-free. Adding a carbon does not relieve anything; it breaks the ring the H needs.

choices.text: Both decarboxylate equally well because both contain a ketone
choices.note: Having a ketone is not enough. Its place, beta to the acid, is what lets the H transfer through the ring.

choices.text: Neither decarboxylates; a ketone cannot assist loss of CO2
choices.note: An ordinary carboxylic acid with no beta carbonyl does hold on to its CO2. A beta ketone is exactly what makes the loss easy.

choices.text: Only the gamma-keto acid decarboxylates, because only its carbonyl and carboxyl are spaced to close a ring, and the product is a cyclic lactone rather than a simple ketone
choices.note: Gamma-keto acids can close toward lactone-type rings, but that keeps the carbon: no CO2 is lost. The beta-keto acid is the one that decarboxylates.

choices.text: Only the beta-keto acid decarboxylates readily on heating; the gamma-keto acid does not, because its carbonyl is too far for a six-membered cyclic transition state
choices.note: Beta puts the C=O where the six-membered ring can form; gamma puts it one carbon too far.

student.lockIt: Only a beta-keto acid, or a malonic acid, loses CO2 easily on heating: the H moves through a six-membered ring.
